title: Lydia
subtitle: 685–546 BC · Sardis, the Mermnad Kings, the First Coins and the Fall of Croesus

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The Heraclids, Gyges and the Mermnad line from Ardys and Alyattes to Croesus

entries.label: The Heraclid kings of Sardis
entries.hint: Herodotus gives Lydia a line of Heraclid kings that ran back twenty-two generations, ending with Candaules, son of Myrsus. Of these kings only the last is anything more than a name in Greek tradition. Lydia emerged from the post-Hittite world as an Anatolian-speaking kingdom on the Hermus and the Pactolus, with a capital at Sardis.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.7–13; Nicolaus of Damascus, FGrH 90; Crawford Greenewalt on early Sardis.

entries.label: Gyges — the usurper king
entries.hint: Gyges, a bodyguard of the last Heraclid, took the throne by a palace murder — the story is told with the ring that makes its wearer invisible — and was confirmed by Delphi. As Gugu of Luddi he appears in Ashurbanipal's inscriptions, sending envoys and Cimmerian captives to Nineveh. Later Herodotus gives him dedications of gold and silver at Delphi. He died fighting the Cimmerians.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.8–14; Ashurbanipal's Prism A and Rassam Cylinder (Gugu of Luddi); Archilochus fr. 19 West (Gyges's wealth).

entries.label: Ardys and Sadyattes
entries.hint: Ardys, Gyges's son, took Priene and fought Miletus, and in his reign the Cimmerians took Sardis except its acropolis. His son Sadyattes continued the war on Miletus. The two reigns span the worst years of the Cimmerian raids, and Lydian power only recovered under their successor.

entries.label: Alyattes — the consolidator
entries.hint: Alyattes drove out the Cimmerians, ended the war against Miletus with a treaty, took Smyrna and fought Cyaxares of Media for six years until an eclipse stopped the battle. He married his daughter Aryenis to Astyages of Media and made the Halys the boundary between the two kingdoms. His enormous burial mound at Bin Tepe was visible from Sardis.

entries.label: Croesus — the last Mermnad
entries.hint: Croesus subjected the Greek cities of the coast to tribute, made friends of Sparta and Egypt, and sent more gold to Delphi than any previous king. Then, convinced by an ambiguous oracle that he would destroy a great empire if he crossed the Halys, he crossed it and was defeated by Cyrus. Sardis fell in 546 BC, and with it the Lydian kingdom.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Cimmerian sack of Sardis, the battle of the Eclipse and Cyrus's war from Pteria to the fall of Sardis

entries.label: The Cimmerians take Sardis
entries.hint: Gyges died fighting the Cimmerians, and the horsemen took Sardis, burning the lower city and holding it for a time, but not the acropolis. The Assyrians read Gyges's fall as the vengeance of the gods on a king who had broken faith with them. Alyattes finally drove them out.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.15–16; Strabo 13.4.8 (Callisthenes); Ashurbanipal's inscriptions on Gyges's death.

entries.label: The battle of the Eclipse
entries.hint: After six years of war between Alyattes and Cyaxares, the armies met by the river Halys when the day went dark in an eclipse, and both sides, taking it as an omen, made peace. The eclipse is dated, from astronomy, to 28 May 585 BC, which gives Greek and Near Eastern history a fixed point. Herodotus says that Thales predicted it.

entries.label: Pteria and Thymbra
entries.hint: Croesus crossed the Halys and fought Cyrus to a draw at Pteria in Cappadocia, then went home to Sardis in the winter to raise a new army from his allies. Cyrus marched after him, meeting him on the plain before Sardis. There the Lydian cavalry was thrown into disorder by Persian camels and driven within the walls.

entries.label: The fall of Sardis
entries.hint: The siege lasted fourteen days. A Mardian soldier, watching a Lydian pick up a dropped helmet on a precipitous part of the acropolis, took the same path, and the Persians climbed the unguarded rock. Croesus was captured. A Greek tradition puts him on a pyre from which Apollo saved him, and in other versions he serves Cyrus as an adviser.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.84–91; Bacchylides 3; Nabonidus Chronicle (Cyrus's campaign in the 'land of Lydia').

entries.label: The revolt of Pactyes
entries.hint: Pactyes, whom Cyrus had left to look after the treasure of Sardis, raised mercenaries on the coast and besieged the Persian governor in the acropolis. Cyrus sent a general, Mazares, who retook Sardis and then enslaved Priene. The revolt ended any chance of a Lydian restoration.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Delphi's blessing of a usurper and the gold and silver standard of Croesus

entries.label: Delphi blesses a usurper
entries.hint: When the Lydians objected to the murder of Candaules, both parties agreed to ask Delphi, which decided for Gyges, adding that the Heraclids would have their vengeance in the fifth generation. The prophecy, that fell on Croesus, was said to have been ignored by the Lydians and their kings. An oracle served as a court of last resort.

entries.label: The Croesus gold and silver standard
entries.hint: Croesus is credited with the first coinage of pure gold and pure silver, struck with the confronted lion and bull in the form of staters of fixed weight, so that the value of gold and silver could be set against each other. The standard was taken over by Persia as the daric and the siglos. Some scholars place the first bimetallic coinage under Darius instead.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.50, 1.94; Robert Wallace, American Journal of Archaeology 91 (1987); Ramage and Craddock, King Croesus' Gold (2000).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Kybebe on the Pactolus and the gold of Croesus at Delphi

entries.label: Kybebe on the Pactolus
entries.hint: The great goddess of Sardis was Kuvava or Kybebe, the Lydian form of the Anatolian mother whom the Greeks called Cybele or Artemis of Sardis. An altar to her stood on the banks of the gold-bearing Pactolus, and her sanctuary was among the buildings burned by the Ionians in 498 BC. The monumental temple of Artemis of Sardis belongs to the fourth century, over an older cult.
entries.note: Herodotus 5.102; Crawford Greenewalt, Sardis excavation reports (the Pactolus altar of Kybebe, 1960s–).

entries.label: Croesus's gifts to Delphi
entries.hint: Croesus gave Delphi 117 ingots of gold, a lion of pure gold, bowls of gold and silver and women's ornaments, after the oracle was tested and found right. The god's response, that if he made war on the Persians he would destroy a great empire, became the most famous ambiguous oracle in Greek tradition.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The mound of Alyattes, the Lydian hoard, the lydion and Croesus on the pyre

entries.label: Marching to pipes and lyres
entries.hint: Herodotus says that when Alyattes invaded the Milesian lands he did so with an army accompanied by syrinxes, harps and aulos players, male and female, high and low. Lydian music was famous among the Greeks, and the 'Lydian mode' of Greek music theory carried its name.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.17; Plato, Republic 398e (Lydian modes); Athenaeus 14.635 on Lydian instruments.

entries.label: The Lydian Hoard
entries.hint: A collection of gold and silver vessels, jewellery and wall paintings looted from tumuli at Güre in Uşak in the 1960s was sold to the Metropolitan Museum of Art and returned to Turkey in 1993 after a long lawsuit. The hoard, a part of the Karun treasure, shows the wealth and the fusion of Lydian, Persian and Greek taste in the sixth and fifth centuries.
entries.note: Metropolitan Museum 'Lydian Hoard' litigation and return (1987–1993); Özgen and Öztürk, The Lydian Treasure (1996).

entries.label: The lydion and marbled ware
entries.hint: Lydian potters made the lydion, a small slender perfume vessel in black and red slips that was sold throughout the Greek world, and a marbled ware with swirling patterns of black and cream. The vessel carried scented oil to Ionian and Greek buyers and was copied by Greek potters.
entries.note: Sardis pottery reports (Hanfmann and Greenewalt); Susan Rotroff on archaic Sardis ceramics.

entries.label: The mound of Alyattes
entries.hint: North of Sardis, on the Gygean lake, stands a tumulus of Alyattes some 355 metres across, the largest on the cemetery of Bin Tepe, a thousand mounds. Herodotus says that its base was of great stones, with markers inscribed with the contributions of traders, craftsmen and young women. The burial chamber, found in 1853, had been robbed.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.93; George Dennis and Ludwig Spiegelthal excavations (1853); Greenewalt on Bin Tepe.

entries.label: Croesus on the pyre
entries.hint: An Athenian red-figure amphora by Myson shows Croesus seated on a pyre, pouring a libation while an attendant lights the fire. It is the earliest known picture of the story of Croesus's rescue by Apollo and was painted within two generations of Sardis's fall.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: A language of Sardis and Solon's warning to a king

entries.label: The Lydian language and alphabet
entries.hint: Lydian was an Anatolian Indo-European language, related to Hittite and Luwian, written in an alphabet of its own derived from the Greek and Phoenician scripts. The surviving inscriptions are short, from Sardis and the Hermus valley, and include coin legends and a few bilinguals.
entries.note: Roberto Gusmani, Lydisches Wörterbuch (1964), and the Sardis epigraphic publications.

entries.label: Solon and Croesus
entries.hint: In Herodotus, Croesus shows his treasures to the Athenian visitor Solon and asks whom he thinks the happiest of men. Solon names ordinary Athenians who died well, and tells Croesus to call no man happy till he is dead. The meeting, which probably never took place, is Herodotus's way of framing the king's fall.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The first coins, the gold of the Pactolus, the Croesus standard and the first retailers

entries.label: The gold of the Pactolus
entries.hint: Gold flakes washed down from Mount Tmolus into the Pactolus, which flowed past the acropolis of Sardis, and were collected in sheepskins and by washing. The electrum the kings had was a native alloy of the river's own gold. The Greeks put the origins of Midas's golden touch in its waters.

entries.label: The first coins
entries.hint: The earliest known coins, small lumps of electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, stamped with a lion's head or striped marks, were struck in Lydia and the neighbouring Ionian cities in the middle or later seventh century. The invention made the weight and fineness of a piece of metal a matter of a stamp. The Ephesian Artemision deposit gives the best find context.
entries.note: D. G. Hogarth, Excavations at Ephesus (1908); Robert Wallace, 'The origin of electrum coinage', American Journal of Archaeology 91 (1987).

entries.label: The first retailers
entries.hint: Herodotus says that the Lydians were the first to coin gold and silver and the first to sell goods by retail (kapeloi). A money economy with shopkeepers and the daily marketplace appears at Sardis for the first time in the sixth century, and the Lydians became proverbially a people of traders.

entries.label: The wealth of Croesus
entries.hint: Croesus's riches became proverbial, 'rich as Croesus' from his time to ours. They came from the Pactolus gold, from the tribute of the Greek cities and from the trade that passed through Sardis, and they funded his dedications at Delphi, Ephesus and Didyma.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The gold refinery of Sardis and the acropolis that fell

entries.label: The acropolis that was thought impregnable
entries.hint: The acropolis of Sardis stood on a steep spur of crumbling stone with terraced walls, and the Lydians thought it so strong that they left a stretch unwatched. Its fall in 546 BC shows how the best defences are only as good as their guards.

entries.label: The gold refinery of Sardis
entries.hint: Excavators at Sardis found a refinery of the Croesus era in the area known as Pactolus North, with crucibles, cupels and cement of salt, used to separate gold from silver in electrum by cementation. It is the earliest known industrial production of pure gold, and made the Croesus standard possible.
entries.note: Andrew Ramage and Paul Craddock, King Croesus' Gold: Excavations at Sardis and the History of Gold Refining (2000).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: Gyges and Nineveh, the oath of the Halys, the alliances against Cyrus and Delphi's gold

entries.label: Gyges and Ashurbanipal
entries.hint: Ashurbanipal's annals say that Gugu of Luddi, a land whose name the Assyrians had not heard, sent envoys after a dream of the god Ashur, with captured Cimmerian chiefs as a gift. Later Gugu sent troops to Egypt to help Psamtik I against Assyria, and Ashurbanipal considered that betrayal the cause of his fall.
entries.note: Ashurbanipal's Prism A and the Rassam Cylinder (Streck, Assurbanipal, 1916).

entries.label: The oath of the Halys
entries.hint: After the eclipse, Syennesis of Cilicia and Labynetus of Babylon mediated a peace between Alyattes and Cyaxares, sealed by a marriage of the Lydian king's daughter Aryenis to the Median prince Astyages and by an oath in which the two kings cut their arms and licked each other's blood.

entries.label: Guest-friendship with Athens
entries.hint: Alcmaeon, an Athenian who helped Croesus's envoys at Delphi, was invited to Sardis and told to carry away as much gold as he could, and he came out in loose robes and boots stuffed with gold, and his mouth full of gold dust. The wealth of the Alcmaeonids was said to date from that day.

entries.label: Alliances against Cyrus
entries.hint: Before crossing the Halys Croesus made alliances with Amasis of Egypt, Labynetus of Babylon (Nabonidus) and Sparta, which were to join him in the next year's campaign. They did not arrive in time, and Cyrus was at the gates of Sardis before the allies could gather.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: The Cimmerian shock, a four-power balance and the end of the Mermnads

entries.label: The Cimmerian shock
entries.hint: The Cimmerian raids broke Phrygia and exposed Lydia for a generation, killed Gyges, burned Sardis and left Anatolia without a strong power in the west. When Alyattes finally drove the horsemen out, Lydia was left as the one major state of western Anatolia.
entries.note: Herodotus 1.15–16; Strabo 1.3.21; Assyrian letters on the Cimmerians.

entries.label: A four-power balance
entries.hint: After the peace on the Halys, four states dominated the Near East: Lydia in the west, Media in the north and east, Babylon in Mesopotamia and Egypt on the Nile, each with dynastic marriage ties and each avoiding war. The balance held for a generation until Cyrus destroyed it.

entries.label: The end of the Mermnads
entries.hint: The fall of Sardis closed a kingdom that had lasted for a century and a half and moved the capital of western Anatolia to the Persian governor in the old palace. Sardis remained a great city, the western end of the Royal Road, but no longer the seat of a king.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Candaules's queen, the daughters who earned their dowries and the Lydians made soft

entries.label: Candaules's queen
entries.hint: In Herodotus's story, Candaules insisted on showing his wife naked to his bodyguard Gyges, and when the queen discovered it she forced Gyges to choose between killing the king and being killed himself. The tale of shame and revenge is told in a Greek frame, with a woman as the instrument of a political change.

entries.label: Daughters who earned their dowries
entries.hint: Herodotus says that among the Lydians all the daughters of ordinary families sold themselves until they had earned a dowry, and then married whom they pleased. He adds that the contributions to Alyattes's tomb were chiefly from such women. The report, written by a Greek outsider, may exaggerate.

entries.label: The Lydians made soft
entries.hint: After the revolt of Pactyes, Croesus is said to have advised Cyrus to forbid the Lydians arms and to make them wear tunics and boots, and to teach them to play the lyre and keep shops so that they would soon become women instead of men. The tale puts the Greek stereotype of the soft Lydian at the moment of conquest, and it is more about Greek ideas than about Lydians.
